characterization_methods.key_findings: The 17Al alloy aged at 550 °C for 10 h gave 815.3 ± 19.1 HV; the 17Al hardness window across all aging conditions spanned 259.8 HV to 924.9 HV (peak at 575 °C/6 h).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Load 9.8 N, dwell 15 s; 5 repeated measurements averaged per sample
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the Vickers hardness of the 17Al samples after different aging treatments (including 550 °C/10 h).

characterization_methods.key_findings: XRD patterns of selected aged samples showed both α-Mn and β-Mn diffraction peaks (co-precipitation of α-Mn and β-Mn); α/D0₃ reflections also present. The 17Al trace shown corresponds to 575 °C/1 h.
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify phase compositions of the alloys / aged samples.

characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy, β-Mn precipitated first along α grain boundaries then within grains as short rods; at 550 °C the α matrix nearly fully transformed to β-Mn by 6 h, and by 10 h a uniform β-Mn matrix was observed.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: SE imaging; 50 µm main-field scale bars with 2–10 µm insets
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify precipitation of secondary phases (α-Mn, β-Mn) and, with EDS, micro-area compositions.
characterization_methods.technique: Scanning electron microscopy (secondary electron imaging) and EDS

characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al alloy, phase maps show the α→β-Mn transformation advancing with aging; after full transformation new BCC and FCC precipitates appear within β-Mn (Fig. 5).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Scanning step size 1.5 µm for low magnification and 0.05 µm for high magnification
characterization_methods.purpose: Resolve constituent phases (α/BCC, β-Mn, α-Mn, FCC) and their distribution after aging.

characterization_methods.key_findings: Fine FCC Cu-rich particles with FCC twins form at the β-Mn interfaces; β-Mn identified by SAED. (TEM was performed on the 15Al 600 °C/6 h and 17Al 575 °C/6 h samples.)

characterization_methods.purpose: Elucidate the microstructures of the ultra-high-hardness alloys and the interfaces between β-Mn and the precipitates.

characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 17Al hardest sample the average nanoindentation hardness was 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa and the β-Mn intrinsic hardness was 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa (measured on the 575 °C/6 h peak sample).

characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn and the micro-hardness distribution of the hardest samples.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by melting raw materials of high purity (>99.9 %) in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere.
The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Plates hot-rolled to a thickness of 4 mm.
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Samples solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching (parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
Solution-treated samples aged at 550 °C for 10 h (within the 525–650 °C / 1, 3, 6, 10 h schedule), followed by water quenching. This is the terminal state of the target sample.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: aging-hardening response / precipitation kinetics of β-Mn

interfaces.interface_notes: The β-Mn is Mn-rich and poor in Al and Cu; its nucleation/growth expels Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix, giving rise to the FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates at the β-Mn interfaces. The content of the FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces decreased with increasing Al content.
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase (proposed aging sequence for the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels).

phases_present.morphology: matrix; the α matrix almost completely transformed into β-Mn (transformavtion complete after 6 h at 550 °C) forming a uniform matrix in SE-SEM
fine precipitates distributed within the β-Mn
fine particles distributed at the interfaces between β-Mn

structures.overall_structure: After aging at 550 °C for 10 h the α (BCC) matrix of the 17Al Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu alloy has nearly/almost completely transformed into the ultra-hard β-Mn phase (transformation completed after 6 h at 550 °C), giving a uniform β-Mn matrix in the SE-SEM image; fine 'new' BCC and FCC (Cu-rich) precipitates are distributed within the β-Mn after full transformation. Increasing Al content (relative to 15Al) slowed the β-Mn precipitation kinetics.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and averaged. Sample condition: 17Al aged at 550 °C for 10 h.

unmapped_findings: 17Al alloy chemical composition (EDS, Table 1): Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 at.% (nominal Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu at.%).

Solution-treated (1100 °C/10 min + oil quench) baseline Vickers hardness of the 17Al alloy = 259.8 ± 1.5 HV (Table 3), i.e. belongs to the parent solution-treatment state rather than the 550 °C/10 h aged sample.

The peak hardness of the 17Al alloy (924.9 ± 25.8 HV) was reached by aging at 575 °C for 6 h, not by the 550 °C/10 h condition; the hardest 17Al sample's intrinsic β-Mn hardness measured by nanoindentation was 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa (average nanoindentation hardness of that sample = 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa).

For the hardest 17Al sample (575 °C/6 h, 924.9 HV), the indentation-measured fracture toughness KIC was 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 (average crack length 22 µm, elastic modulus 175 GPa); these are not values of the 550 °C/10 h sample.
β-Mn micro-area composition in the hardest 17Al sample (SEM-EDS, Fig. 14): Mn 36.2, Al 16.3, Cu 2.6 at.% (measured on the 575 °C/6 h sample, not the 550 °C/10 h sample).

The volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich + BCC precipitates in the 17Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 10 h was 4.7 % with an average Vickers hardness of 833.2 HV (a different aging condition from the 550 °C/10 h sample).
Proposed general aging phase-evolution sequence for the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steels: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase.
